Ingredients
3 tbsp of sugar
5 tbsp of soybean paste; if you don’t have it, use miso paste (#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/soybean-paste)
1 tsp of sesame butter or tahini paste (#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/sesame-paste)
1 tsp of garlic powder(#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/garlic-powder)
1 tsp of fine chili powder(#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/chili-powder)
1 pieces of red fermented bean curd(#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/cantonese-bean-curd)
1/4 tsp of five spice powder(Product Link - https://curatedkitchenware.com/products/five-spice-powder-25g)
3 tbsp of water
1 tsp of dark soy sauce(#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/dark-soy-sauce)

Homemade Hoisin sauce is actually super simple, but the main purpose of this recipe is to show you how I break down the formula and came up with the recipe. Once you understand the “whys” behind the “hows,” you’ll be able to recreate almost any commercial sauce from scratch.

First, let’s see what hoisin sauce is made of. After comparing the ingredient list of the 2 most popular brands on the market, Haitian and Lee Kum Kee, I found that hoisin sauce is basically made with sugar and fermented soybeans, then layered with garlic, sesame, fermented bean curd, and chilies for extra flavor. Ingredients can vary from brand to brand, but it doesn't matter; as long as you know the main ingredients, you can play around and adjust however you like.

Then I compared the ingredients between hoisin sauce and soybean paste. Their main ingredients are almost the same. The difference is that hoisin sauce lists sugar first. As for the soybean paste, it doesn't include garlic, sesame, chilies, or fermented bean curd. So, in other words, Hoisin sauce is essentially a sweeter version of soybean paste with some extra complexity.


I know some of you are probably thinking: “Why bother with seven different ingredients when I can just grab a bottle from the store?” Well, with homemade hoisin sauce, you can adjust the taste based on your preference, such as reducing the sugar amount, increasing the chili spice kick, or the nutty taste. Also, It’s always empowering to know what’s in your sauces and how to make them.

For the real adventurous cooks — if you want to go all the way from scratch, including fermenting your own soybeans, drop a comment below. I’d love to make a full video about it!

There's a saying: If a Cantonese grandma makes this for you, you've officially been adopted. Back in the days when meat was expensive, canned fried dace used to be considered a luxury. So it's the kind of meal you cook for the people you love.
﻿
When I was a kid, I could never understand why adults loved bitter melon so much. It was bitter... and I was convinced they were all pretending to enjoy it.

Then one day, something changed. Maybe I finally grew up, or maybe my taste buds did.  Suddenly, the bitterness wasn't unpleasant anymore. It was refreshing, comforting, and surprisingly addictive. Now it's one of my favorite vegetables, especially when it's cooked with fried dace and fermented black beans.

Ingredients

400g of bitter melon, cut into bite-sized pieces
1 can of fried dace with fermented black beans (#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/canned-fried-dace)
2 cloves of garlic, diced
2 tsp of soy sauce (#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/light-soy-sauce)
2 tsp of oyster sauce (#ad Amazon Link - https://geni.us/premium-oyster-sauce)
1/2 cup of water
2 tbsp of diced scallion
2 tbsp of diced cilantro
2 tbsp of diced Thai bird eye chilies

Quarter the bitter melon, remove the inner seeds. Then cut it into bite-sized pieces. 

Roughly cut the fried dace into bite-sized pieces.

Add the bitter melon, fried dace, diced garlic, soy sauce, oyster sauce, and water to a clay pot. Put on the lid, turn the heat to medium, and cook for 10 minutes.

Garnish with diced scallion, cilantro, and Thai bird eye chilies. Serve with white rice.

The secret to make the best HongKong Bubble Milk Tea isn't the bubbles—it's the tea and the way you make the tea.  Make sure you use this traditional Hong Kong Lā Chá (拉茶) technique, also known as pulling the tea. The tea is poured back and forth through a silk stocking filter to create a smoother, richer, and more aromatic flavor. Then it's combined with evaporated milk, sugar, and homemade brown sugar boba for the perfect balance of creamy, silky, and chewy textures.
